title: Functions and Cardinality (Funktionen und Kardinalität)
summary: This unit develops functions, inverse functions (Umkehrfunktionen), injectivity and surjectivity (Injektivität und Surjektivität), function composition (Komposition von Funktionen), permutations (Permutationen), orbits and cycles (Orbits und Zyklen), images and preimages (Bilder und Urbilder), and function-induced equivalence relations (funktionsinduzierte Äquivalenzrelationen). It then compares sets using injections and bijections, introduces countability (Abzählbarkeit), and develops Cantor’s diagonal argument (Cantors Diagonalargument) for uncountable sets (überabzählbare Mengen). It also covers the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem, the Cantor pairing function, cardinal arithmetic and currying, and the continuum hypothesis.
keyFacts: A function is left-total and right-unique.
A function is injective if each target has at most one preimage, and surjective if each target element has at least one preimage.
A function is bijective if and only if each element of the codomain has exactly one preimage.
The converse relation of a function is itself a function defined on the entire codomain if and only if the original function is bijective.
For bijective functions, (g ∘ f)⁻¹ = f⁻¹ ∘ g⁻¹; the order reverses when taking the inverse.
A permutation is a bijective self-map.
In a self-map, each node has exactly one outgoing edge; a fixed point is a self-loop.
For a finite self-map, injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity are equivalent; its graph then consists of disjoint cycles.
Preimages preserve unions, intersections, and set differences; images preserve unions without any additional assumptions.
For every subset X, f⁻¹(f(X)) = X if and only if f is injective.
The relation a ≡f a′ if and only if f(a) = f(a′) is an equivalence relation.
|A| ≤ |B| means that an injection A → B exists; |A| = |B| means that a bijection exists.
By the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem, one injection in each direction suffices to conclude that the sets have the same cardinality.
Countable means |A| ≤ |ℕ| and includes finite sets.
The natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, and finite words over a countable alphabet are countable.
The Cantor pairing function shows that ℕ × ℕ is countable.
For every set A, |A| < |𝒫(A)|; Cantor’s diagonal argument shows that no map A → 𝒫(A) is surjective.
The set of infinite binary sequences and the real numbers are uncountable.
For sets A, B, and C, C^(A×B) is bijective to both (C^B)^A and (C^A)^B.
The continuum hypothesis asserts that there is no cardinality strictly between |ℕ| and |ℝ|; Cantor’s theorem alone does not decide it.

review.notes: Alle 43 Fragen geprüft. Antworten, Distraktoren, Erklärungen, Selbstständigkeit, Diagramme und verify-Skripte sind fachlich/formal stimmig; keine Korrekturen oder Ersetzungen nötig.

questions.prompt: Which condition describes a bijective function $f:A\to B$?

options.text: Each element of $B$ has at most one preimage in $A$.
Each element of $A$ has at least two images in $B$.
Each element of $B$ has exactly one preimage in $A$.
Each element of $A$ has at least one preimage in $B$.

questions.explanation: Bijectivity means that each codomain element is hit exactly once. “At most one preimage” alone describes only injectivity.

questions.prompt: The converse relation $f^\top$ of a function $f:A\to B$ is a function $B\to A$ if and only if $f$ is bijective.
questions.explanation: The inverse relation must assign exactly one preimage to every element of $B$. This holds precisely when the function is both surjective and injective.

questions.prompt: For $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$, we have $(g\circ f)(x)=___$.
questions.explanation: In $g\circ f$, $f$ is applied first, followed by $g$. Therefore, the result is $g(f(x))$.

questions.prompt: What is a permutation of a set $A$?

options.text: An injective function from $A$ into another set.
A surjective function from $A$ into a superset.

questions.explanation: A permutation is a bijective self-map: its domain and codomain are both $A$.

questions.prompt: Consider a self-map $f:A\to A$. Select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A fixed point is an element $a$ such that $f(a)=a$.
Every node in every self-map has exactly one incoming edge.
Every node in the graph has exactly one outgoing edge.

questions.explanation: The function property guarantees exactly one outgoing edge from each node. Incoming edges may be absent or may occur more than once; exactly one incoming edge per node holds only for a permutation.

questions.prompt: For every function $f:A\to B$, it automatically holds that $f(A)=B$.
questions.explanation: $f(A)$ contains only values that are actually attained and is always a subset of $B$. Equality holds if and only if $f$ is surjective.

questions.prompt: For an arbitrary function $f:A\to B$, $f^{-1}(Y)$ for $Y\subseteq B$ is the set of …

options.text: the individual inverse values of $f$ for each element of $Y$.
all $b\in B$ that have a preimage in $Y$.
all elements of $A$ whose images lie outside $Y$.

questions.explanation: The preimage of a set consists of the inputs whose function values lie in that set. This preimage operation is defined even when $f$ is not bijective.

questions.prompt: Select all correct descriptions of cardinality comparisons. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $|A|<|B|$ means that $|A|\leq|B|$ holds and no bijection between $A$ and $B$ exists.
$|A|=|B|$ means that there is a bijection $A\to B$.
$|A|\leq|B|$ means that there is a bijection $B\to A$.
$|A|\leq|B|$ means that there is an injection $A\to B$.

questions.explanation: Cardinality relations are defined using injections or bijections. A bijection $B\to A$ would express equal cardinality rather than a strict inequality.

questions.prompt: When is a set $A$ called countable?

options.text: If and only if there is a bijection $A\to\mathbb R$.
If and only if $A$ is infinite.
If and only if $|A|\leq|\mathbb N|$ holds.
If and only if $A$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb N$.

questions.explanation: Countable includes both finite and countably infinite sets. The key condition is the existence of an injection into the natural numbers.

questions.prompt: Although $2\mathbb N$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb N$, we have $|2\mathbb N|=|\mathbb N|$.
questions.explanation: The map $n\mapsto 2n$ is a bijection from $\mathbb N$ onto the positive even numbers. For infinite sets, a proper subset need not have smaller cardinality.

questions.prompt: Which node is a fixed point in this self-map?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  a((a)) --> b((b))
  b --> b
  c((c)) --> a
context.caption: Directed graph of a self-map

questions.explanation: A fixed point has a self-loop, that is, an edge from itself to itself. In the diagram, only $b$ has this property.

questions.prompt: For $A=\{1,2,3\}$, the self-maps $f,g:A\to A$ are given in the table. We have $(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))$: so apply $g$ first, then $f$. Find the value tuple $((f\circ g)(1),(f\circ g)(2),(f\circ g)(3))$.

context.caption: Value tables for the self-maps $f$ and $g$ on $A=\{1,2,3\}$.

questions.explanation: From the table: for $x=1$, $f(g(1))=f(1)=2$; for $x=2$, $f(g(2))=f(3)=1$; and for $x=3$, $f(g(3))=f(2)=3$. Therefore, the value tuple is $(2,1,3)$.

questions.prompt: The map $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb N$ is defined by $f(z)=2z+1$ for $z\geq0$ and $f(z)=-2z$ for $z<0$. What is $f(-2)$?
questions.explanation: $-2<0$, so the second case applies: $f(-2)=-2\cdot(-2)=4$.

questions.prompt: For a function $f:A\to B$, $f(f^{-1}(Y))=Y$ holds for every $Y\subseteq B$ if and only if $f$ is surjective.
questions.explanation: The image of a preimage can contain only values from $Y$. If every value in $B$ is attained, then each $Y\subseteq B$ is fully recovered; without surjectivity, this fails for sets containing an unattained value.

questions.prompt: Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function. Select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: Images preserve unions, and preimages preserve unions, intersections, and set differences. In general, images preserve intersections only as an inclusion, not as an equality.

questions.prompt: The Cantor pairing function is $p(n,m)=m+\frac{(m+n-1)(m+n-2)}{2}$. Compute $p(2,3)$.
questions.explanation: Substitution gives $3+\frac{(3+2-1)(3+2-2)}{2}=3+\frac{4\cdot3}{2}=9$.

questions.prompt: What is the preimage of $\{r\}$ under the function shown?
questions.explanation: The preimage of $\{r\}$ contains all inputs whose arrows end at $r$. These are $a_1$ and $a_2$.

questions.prompt: Let $f:A\to A$ be a self-map on a finite set. If its graph consists only of disjoint cycles, what property does $f$ have?

options.text: $f$ is a function only if every cycle has length 1.
$f$ must have at least one node with no outgoing edge.

questions.explanation: For a finite self-map, injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity are equivalent. Disjoint cycles ensure that each node has exactly one predecessor and one successor.

questions.prompt: For $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=x^2$, and $g:\mathbb R_{\geq0}\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}$, $g(x)=x^2$: select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: $f$ is bijective because every $x$ has a square root.
$f$ is not surjective because no negative real number is attained.

questions.explanation: On all of $\mathbb R$, for example, $-2$ and $2$ have the same image, and negative values are not in the image. On the nonnegative reals, squaring is bijective, with the square root as its inverse.

questions.prompt: Which statement about $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ follows from the Cantor pairing function?

options.text: $\mathbb N\times\mathbb N$ has the same cardinality as $\mathbb R$.

questions.explanation: The pairing function assigns a unique positive natural number to each pair of positive natural numbers, and it is bijective.

questions.prompt: Which directed cycle repeats in the orbit shown?

context.caption: An orbit with an initial path and a cycle

questions.explanation: The orbit starts with the path $1\to2\to3$ and then enters the cycle $3\to4\to5\to3$.

questions.prompt: In cycle notation, $(1,2,3)$ means that …
questions.explanation: A cycle sends each element to the next; the last element is mapped back to the first.

questions.prompt: Let $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$ be functions not already known to be bijective. From $g\circ f=\operatorname{Id}_A$ alone, it follows that $g$ and $f$ are inverses of each other.
questions.explanation: Without prior bijectivity, one identity equation alone is not enough. Only both equations together guarantee that the functions are inverses of each other.

questions.prompt: Let $f:A\to B$. Select all conditions equivalent to the injectivity of $f$. The equalities are required to hold for all appropriate subsets; more than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: Injectivity prevents distinct inputs from merging when taking images of intersections or differences. Option c would require even the empty set to have the same image as $A$.

questions.prompt: Let $f(1)=f(2)=r$, $X=\{1\}$, and $X'=\{2\}$. Find the pair $(f(X\cap X'),\ f(X)\cap f(X'))$.
questions.explanation: $X$ and $X'$ are disjoint, so $f(X\cap X')=\varnothing$. Both images contain $r$, so their intersection is $\{r\}$.

questions.prompt: Which statement holds for the two maps in the displayed decomposition of an arbitrary function $f$?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["A"] -->|"q: surjective"| Q["Quotient A / ≡f"]
  Q -->|"f̃: injective"| B["B"]
  A -->|"f"| B
context.caption: Factorization of a function through its equivalence classes

options.text: $q$ is always surjective and $\tilde f$ is always injective.
$q$ is always injective and $\tilde f$ is always surjective.
Both maps are defined only when $f$ is bijective.
The decomposition forces $f$ to be bijective.

questions.explanation: The quotient map sends each element to its equivalence class and is therefore surjective. The map from classes to function values is well-defined and injective.

questions.prompt: A function $f:A\to B$ defines $a\equiv_f a'$ if and only if $f(a)=f(a')$. What does the equivalence class $[a]_f$ describe?

options.text: All elements of $B$ that have a preimage under $f$.
All elements of $A$ with the same function value as $a$.
All elements of $A$ that differ from $a$.

questions.explanation: The class groups exactly those inputs whose function value agrees with $f(a)$. It is also the preimage of the singleton set $\{f(a)\}$.

questions.prompt: For a function $f:A\to B$, $f(A\setminus X)=B\setminus f(X)$ holds for every $X\subseteq A$ if and only if $f$ is bijective.
questions.explanation: For a bijection, every value in $B$ has exactly one preimage, so the images of the two complementary parts are exactly complementary. Without bijectivity, this equality can fail.

questions.prompt: A map assigns the sets $S_1=\{1,3\}$, $S_2=\{1\}$, and $S_3=\{1,2,3\}$ to the indices $1,2,3$. Compute $D=\{i\in\{1,2,3\}\mid i\notin S_i\}$.

context.caption: Candidate sets and their diagonal positions

questions.explanation: For $i=1$ and $i=3$, $i$ belongs to $S_i$; for $i=2$, $2$ does not belong to $S_2$. Therefore, $D=\{2\}$.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about countability. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The finite words over a countable alphabet form a countable set.
The set of finite tuples of natural numbers is uncountable.

questions.explanation: The rational numbers can be compared with $\mathbb N$ using injections and the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem. Finite words over a countable alphabet form a countable set, whereas the real numbers are uncountable.

questions.prompt: There are injections $A\to B$ and $B\to A$. Which theorem lets us conclude that $A$ and $B$ have the same cardinality?

options.text: Theorem about the Cantor pairing function

questions.explanation: The Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem states that injections in both directions guarantee the existence of a bijection. The two injections need not be inverses of each other.

questions.prompt: What does the continuum hypothesis assert?

options.text: There is no cardinality strictly between $|\mathbb N|$ and $|\mathbb R|$.
Every infinite set has the same cardinality as $\mathbb R$.
Cantor’s theorem proves that there is a cardinality between $|\mathbb N|$ and $|\mathbb R|$.

questions.explanation: The hypothesis rules out a cardinality strictly between the natural numbers and the real numbers. Cantor’s theorem alone does not settle this question.

questions.prompt: Let $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$ be bijections, with $A=\{1,2,3\}$, $B=\{u,v,w\}$, and $C=\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$. Suppose $f(1)=v$, $f(2)=w$, $f(3)=u$, and $g(u)=\beta$, $g(v)=\gamma$, $g(w)=\alpha$. What is $(g\circ f)^{-1}(\gamma)$?
questions.explanation: We have $(g\circ f)(1)=g(v)=\gamma$. Therefore, the unique preimage of $\gamma$ under the composition is the number $1$.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{a,b,c,d,e\}$, let $f(a)=x$, $f(b)=y$, $f(c)=x$, $f(d)=z$, and $f(e)=y$. The relation $u\sim v$ holds if and only if $f(u)=f(v)$. Which partition consists of the equivalence classes?
questions.explanation: Equal function values determine the classes: $a$ and $c$ map to $x$, $b$ and $e$ map to $y$, and $d$ alone maps to $z$. The classes form a partition of $A$.

questions.prompt: A finite set $A$ has $3$ elements. Its power set satisfies $|\mathcal P(A)|=2^{|A|}$. What pair $(|A|,|\mathcal P(A)|)$ results, and which strict inequality confirms Cantor’s theorem in this case?
questions.explanation: The power set has $2^3=8$ elements. Thus, its cardinality is strictly greater than that of $A$, as Cantor’s theorem requires.

questions.prompt: Programs are finite strings over a countable alphabet, and the real numbers are uncountable. Select all conclusions that follow. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The set of programs is uncountable.
The set of all such programs is at most countable.
There are real numbers that cannot be computed by any such program.
Every real number can be represented by a program because programs can be arbitrarily long.

questions.explanation: Finite strings over a countable alphabet form a countable set. Since the real numbers are uncountable, programs cannot compute all real numbers.

questions.prompt: The Collatz map is $c(n)=n/2$ for even $n$ and $c(n)=3n+1$ for odd $n$. Compute $c^5(5)$, where $c^5$ means applying the map five times.
questions.explanation: The sequence is $5\to16\to8\to4\to2\to1$. After five applications, the value is $1$.

questions.prompt: Let $|A|=2$, $|B|=3$, and $|C|=2$. Use $(|C|^{|B|})^{|A|}=|C|^{|A|\cdot|B|}$ to compute the common value.
questions.explanation: $(2^3)^2=8^2=64$, and likewise $2^{2\cdot3}=2^6=64$. This is the cardinality rule that follows from currying.

questions.prompt: For $A=\{1,2,3\}$, let $S_1=\{1,3\}$, $S_2=\{1\}$, and $S_3=\{1,2,3\}$. Construct $D=\{i\in A\mid i\notin S_i\}$. Which set do you obtain?

context.caption: Three candidate sets and the diagonal positions to check

questions.explanation: At diagonal position $1$, $1$ is in $S_1$; at position $2$, $2$ is absent from $S_2$; and at position $3$, $3$ is in $S_3$. Therefore, only $2$ belongs to $D$.

questions.prompt: For each fixed positive $k$, suppose $\mathbb N^k$ is countable, and suppose $\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}\mathbb N^k$ is also countable. Select all correct conclusions. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The set of all infinite sequences of natural numbers is countable.
A countable union of countable sets is always uncountable.
The set of all finite tuples of natural numbers is countable.

questions.explanation: The union over all positive finite lengths consists exactly of the nonempty finite tuples, and the case $k=2$ consists of ordered pairs. Infinite sequences form a different set from finite tuples.

questions.prompt: Suppose $|\mathbb N|<|2^{\mathbb N}|=|\mathbb R|<|2^{\mathbb R}|$. Select all statements that follow. More than one answer may be correct.
questions.explanation: The first three statements follow directly from the given cardinality chain. The last contradicts the strict inequality that Cantor’s theorem gives for every set.

questions.prompt: Let $f:\{1,2\}\to\{r,g,b\}$ with $f(1)=r$ and $f(2)=g$. For $Y=\{r,b\}$, find the pair $(f^{-1}(Y), f(f^{-1}(Y)))$.
questions.explanation: Only $1$ maps to an element of $Y$, so $f^{-1}(Y)=\{1\}$. Its image is $\{r\}$; the value $b$ is missing because it is not in the image of $f$.

questions.prompt: Let $A=\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ and $f:A\to\{x,y,z,w\}$ with $f(a)=x$, $f(b)=y$, $f(c)=x$, $f(d)=z$, and $f(e)=y$. The relation $u\sim v$ holds if and only if $f(u)=f(v)$. Find the pair $(|A/{\sim}|,|\operatorname{im}(f)|)$.
questions.explanation: The classes are $\{a,c\}$, $\{b,e\}$, and $\{d\}$, so the quotient has three elements. The image is $\{x,y,z\}$ and also has three elements; $w$ is not attained.

questions.prompt: You assign RFID IDs to library books. Each book gets exactly one ID, different books get different IDs, and the scanner can also read IDs that are not currently assigned to any book. Which property is guaranteed for the assignment from books to IDs?

options.text: It is injective: different books have different IDs.
It defines an equivalence relation on the books.
It is bijective: every readable ID belongs to exactly one book.
It is surjective: every readable ID belongs to a book.

questions.explanation: The assignment is injective because no RFID code belongs to two different books. The existence of readable, unassigned IDs shows that it is not surjective.

questions.prompt: An encryption program replaces each letter of a 26-letter alphabet with exactly one letter. Every letter of the alphabet is used exactly once as an output. What makes reliable decryption with a lookup table possible?

options.text: The map is only injective; some output letters may be missing.
The map is an equivalence relation between letters.
The map is only surjective; multiple letters may have the same code.
The map is a permutation; its inverse function restores the letters.

questions.explanation: Since each letter occurs exactly once as an output, the map is bijective and therefore a permutation. Its inverse function uniquely maps each encrypted letter back to the original letter.

questions.prompt: You choose a four-digit PIN. Each digit can be any number from 0 to 9, and leading zeros are allowed. How many different PINs are there?
questions.explanation: Each of the four positions has 10 possibilities, independently of the others. In total, there are $10^4=10\,000$ PINs.

questions.prompt: A digital board game has only finitely many game states. A fixed programmed rule leads from each state to exactly one next state; several states may lead to the same one. Is it true that if you keep making moves, eventually a state repeats, and from then on the same loop runs repeatedly?
questions.explanation: The fixed rule is a self-map of the finite set of game states. Repeated application must eventually revisit a state. Once this happens, the orbit continues in a cycle.

questions.prompt: An online shop assigns a color to each product. You activate the “red” filter, and the shop displays all products whose assigned color is red. Which mathematical operation describes this selection?

options.text: The preimage of the set {red}: all products mapped to red.
The inverse function: each product is assigned a unique color.
The image of the set {red}: all colors mapped from red.
A permutation of the products that changes their order.

questions.explanation: The filter selects all products whose function value lies in {red}. This is the preimage of the color set. The color assignment does not need to have an inverse function.

questions.prompt: Your spreadsheet has a data range with 8 rows and 17 columns. How many cells does the range contain?
questions.explanation: Each row contains 17 cells, and there are 8 rows. So there are $8\cdot17=136$ cells.

questions.prompt: A CRM imports contacts and groups two rows together exactly when their normalized email addresses are equal. What mathematical structure underlies this grouping?

options.text: A function-induced equivalence relation: contacts with the same function value belong to the same class.
An inverse function: each group maps back to exactly one original row.
A permutation: each row is moved to a different row.
A bijection: each email address belongs to exactly one contact row.

questions.explanation: Normalization maps each row to an email address. The relation “having the same function value” is an equivalence relation; its classes contain exactly the rows with the same address.

questions.prompt: A game menu has 9 optional settings that can each be switched on or off independently. How many different on/off configurations are possible?
questions.explanation: Each setting has two states, and all states can be combined freely. Thus there are $2^9=512$ configurations, corresponding to the subsets of a 9-element set.

questions.prompt: Two applications use different ID formats. For the mathematically considered sets of possible IDs, there is an injective conversion from format A to B and an injective conversion from B to A. The two conversions are not constructed as inverse functions. What follows?

options.text: Nothing can be concluded about cardinality unless a bijection is given.
The two sets of IDs have the same cardinality.
Format A necessarily has fewer possible IDs than format B.
The conversions must be inverses of each other.

questions.explanation: By the Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem, injections in both directions suffice to conclude that a bijection exists and the sets have the same cardinality. The two injections need not be inverses of each other.

questions.prompt: A theoretical simulator can set a parameter exactly to any real number in the interval [0,1]. Programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet. Which conclusion follows from comparing the cardinalities?

options.text: Programs and real numbers have the same cardinality because both sets are infinite.
The set of programs is uncountable because there can be arbitrarily many program lengths.
There are real parameter values that no program can compute exactly.
Every real number can be represented by a program because programs can be arbitrarily long.

questions.explanation: The set of finite programs over a finite alphabet is countable, whereas [0,1] is uncountable. Therefore, programs cannot compute every real value in the interval exactly.
